title: The Scalar UDF Hiding in Your WHERE Clause
description: A scalar UDF in the WHERE clause runs per row and blocks parallelism and good estimates; inline the logic so the query optimizes normally. Why it matters: reusable business-logic functions are a natural, common design choice -- but placed in a WHERE clause, a scalar UDF can turn a fast query into a serial, row-by-row disaster at scale.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
Imagine you're a librarian, and someone asks you to find every book published after 1990. If the library's card catalog is sorted by publication year, you can flip straight to the 1990 card and grab every book after it — done in seconds. That's what a database index lets SQL Server do: it keeps a sorted 'card catalog' of a column so it can jump straight to the rows you want instead of checking every single book on every shelf.

Now imagine the same request, but this time the librarian is handed a weird rule: 'find every book where (published year times 0.9) is greater than 1800.' The card catalog is sorted by plain publication year, not by 'year times 0.9', so the sorted catalog is useless for this version of the question. The only way to answer it is to walk every shelf, pick up every single book, do the math on each one, and check if it passes. That is exactly what happens in SQL Server when you write a WHERE clause like `WHERE fn_NetAmount(Total) > 900` instead of `WHERE Total > 1000`. Even though the two are mathematically identical, the second one lets SQL Server use the sorted index (the card catalog) and the first one forces it to check every row by hand. This property — whether a predicate can use an index seek or not — is called being **SARGable** (short for 'Search ARGument-able'). A SARGable predicate compares a plain, untouched column to a value. As soon as you wrap the column in a function, a calculation, or a conversion, you've broken that property and the optimizer falls back to reading everything.

That alone would slow a query down, but this lesson pairs it with a second, nastier problem: the wrapping function here isn't just an inline calculation, it's a **scalar user-defined function (UDF)** — a little piece of T-SQL code someone wrote once so they wouldn't have to repeat the same formula everywhere. Scalar UDFs feel like they should be cheap: they look like a single function call, the same way calling `Math.round()` in a C# or Java program feels cheap. But SQL Server's query engine works in **sets** — it's built from the ground up to process thousands of rows in bulk, using highly optimized, vectorized operations. A scalar UDF breaks that model completely. For every single row, SQL Server has to pause the set-based machinery, spin up something closer to a tiny stored-procedure call, run your UDF's logic row-by-row, get the answer back, and then resume. If your table has 400,000 rows, that is 400,000 tiny 'function calls', each with its own overhead — and older or non-inlined UDFs (declared with `INLINE = OFF`, meaning SQL Server is not allowed to try to unpack the function's logic and merge it into the main query plan) can't be optimized away at all.

There's a second, more subtle cost that trips people up in production: a query containing a non-inlined scalar UDF is usually forced to run on a **single CPU thread**, even on a server with 32 or 64 cores sitting idle. Normally, when SQL Server scans a big table, it can split the work across multiple threads and parallelize it — like handing different sections of the library to several assistants at once. But the engine can't safely parallelize arbitrary procedural code hidden inside a scalar function (it might do something like access data outside the row, and guaranteeing correctness across threads becomes too risky), so it just refuses to try. The result is a query that looks simple, returns a small result set, and yet crawls, using one lonely CPU core to grind through hundreds of thousands of rows one function call at a time.

Why does this happen in the real world so often? Because scalar UDFs are a genuinely reasonable design choice from a software engineering point of view: 'don't repeat yourself' says wrap the net-amount formula in one function so every report uses the same calculation. Nobody sets out to write a slow query — they set out to avoid duplicating a formula in ten different SELECT statements. The trap is that this very reasonable code-reuse instinct, applied inside a WHERE clause, silently turns a fast, index-friendly filter into a slow, single-threaded, full-table scan. And because the query still returns correct results — just slowly — it can sit in production for a long time before anyone notices, especially if it was fast back when the table only had a few thousand rows. As the table grows, the cost of scanning and calling the function per row grows right along with it, until one day a report that used to take a second takes twenty.

What you'll actually observe when you look at the execution plan is a giveaway: instead of a cheap **Index Seek** (jump straight to the matching rows), you'll see an **Index Scan** or **Table Scan** (read every row), often with an unusually high estimated cost for such a small result set, and the plan will show no parallelism operators even though the table is large. The fix in cases like this one is almost always the same: figure out what the function is actually doing mathematically, and rewrite the WHERE clause so the column stands alone, moving the calculation to the other side of the comparison. `fn_NetAmount(Total) > 900`, once you unwrap it, is just `Total * 0.9 > 900`, which is simple algebra away from `Total > 1000` — a plain, SARGable comparison that the index on `Total` can seek directly. When the logic genuinely needs to be reused across many queries, better alternatives than a scalar UDF exist, such as an inline table-valued function (which SQL Server can 'unfold' into the main query, unlike a scalar UDF) or a computed column that's persisted and indexed.

## Scenario
A report filters on a 'net amount' using a helper function:
`SELECT OrderId, Total FROM Orders WHERE fn_NetAmount(Total) > 900`.
It returns only ~300 rows from 400k but is dramatically slow and never goes parallel.

## Why it's slow
Two compounding problems. First, wrapping a column in **any** expression (here, a function of `Total`) is **non-SARGable** — the optimizer can't seek `IX_Orders_Total`, so it **scans** every row. Second, a **scalar UDF** is invoked **once per row** with heavy per-call overhead, and (this one is declared `WITH INLINE = OFF`, so SQL Server's automatic UDF inlining can't rescue it) it also **forces the whole plan to run serially**. 400k hidden function calls.

## What to look for
- An **Index Scan** instead of a Seek, touching all 400k rows.
- No parallelism, and a plan that hides the true cost of the per-row function calls.

## The concept
Don't put scalar functions on columns in a predicate. Here the function is just `Total * 0.9`, so `fn_NetAmount(Total) > 900` is algebraically identical to the **SARGable** `Total > 1000`. Rewriting it lets SQL Server seek the index, read only the ~300 matching rows, and drop the per-row UDF entirely. When logic is genuinely reusable, prefer an **inline table-valued function** or a computed/persisted column over a scalar UDF.
startingQuery: SELECT OrderId, Total FROM Orders WHERE e_01_scalar_udf_predicate.fn_NetAmount(Total) > 900;
hints: The column Total is buried inside a scalar function, so the index on Total can't be seeked.
fn_NetAmount(Total) is Total * 0.9. Solve the inequality for Total itself.
Total * 0.9 > 900 is the same as Total > 1000. Rewrite: SELECT OrderId, Total FROM Orders WHERE Total > 1000;
